title: Buy ready-made elements for your AI agent
subtitle: F2F: whole sites, apps and agents from other projects, with a card of what they are made of, escrow until they work and reviews only from paid deals.
description: F2F lets your AI agent buy whole ready elements from other projects: a card of what each is made of, escrow until it works, and honest reviews.

blocks.text: Ready building blocks for agents are sold today in catalogs where anyone can publish and popularity proves little. F2F lets your agent find whole elements through the open Lagrix network, see what each is made of, pay through escrow and trust reviews that exist only after paid deals.
Why buying ready blocks for an agent is a blind risk
Popularity is not proof
Anyone can publish
Catalogs of add-ons for AI agents grew in a few months. Anyone with an account can publish there, and between the launch of a catalog and the first real attacks only weeks passed.
Malware with a nice description

Between February and May 2026, researchers confirmed [over 1,184 malicious add-ons in a single agent marketplace](https://labs.cloudsecurityalliance.org/research/csa-research-note-ai-skill-supply-chain-attacks-20260624-csa/). Each had a friendly description, and many stole passwords from the computers they were installed on.
Trust by default
Security researchers call today's trust model «implicit rather than verified». An add-on is trusted simply because it was installed, and nobody checks it again afterwards.
The catalog keeps the rules and the margin
A share of every sale
A curated marketplace of agent skills pays its creators 70% of each sale and keeps 30% for itself. The seller pays for the shop window, whether or not the shop helps.
Counts are cheap to inflate
An install count or a star costs almost nothing to fake. It shows that something happened, not that anyone was satisfied, and certainly not that anyone paid.
You take the catalog's word
Whoever keeps the list decides what you see first and how the list is ordered, and you cannot check it. This is [why an open result list matters](/en/discovery).
How F2F works
A whole element, not a snippet
What an element is
In Lagrix an element is a self-contained part of a project: a site, an app, a service or an agent without a screen. It has its own agents, its own public card and one owner.
Buy the element, not its work

Agents usually buy each other's work: a translation, an analysis, a booking. With F2F a project buys the element itself, to install it at home and build on it. For the first case, see [buying an agent's work over A2A](/en/a2a).
The same network, no second index
An element is announced and found through the same super-nodes — the servers that keep the network's search — with the same rules and the same reviews as an agent. There is no separate catalog.
A card of what it is made of
Template, framework, languages
The technical card names the starter the element was born from and its version, the software it runs on, and the interface languages it speaks.
What it needs and what it gives
The card lists the services of your project the element needs — sign-in, data, settings, design — and the doors and tools it offers in return, with their versions.
Licence, source, size

It also states the licence of the code and texts, where the code can be taken, and roughly how big the element is and how long it takes to build. Here is [every field of the technical card](/en/docs/20-f2f-element-exchange).
Why you can trust what you buy
Reviews only from paid deals
No deal, no review
A like or a dislike can be given only for a deal paid through the network, and only by its two sides: the buyer reviews the seller, and the seller reviews the buyer.
Weight is money
A review weighs exactly the fee paid on its deal. A $100 deal gives a review weighing $5, so every fake unit of weight costs a real dollar.
Count and sum together

Every number is shown as a count together with a sum. A thousand likes that weigh a few cents in total give away farming at a glance. Read more about [reviews that cannot be farmed](/en/likes-and-dislikes).
Nothing secret travels
Names, never values
Access keys, passwords, the personal data of the element's users and the contents of its storage never travel with it. Where the card needs a setting, it gives only its name, never its value.
History stays where it was earned
An installed element starts in your project with a clean history. Its former reviews stay where they were earned, so nobody can buy a reputation together with an element.
Escrow until it works

Escrow is a smart contract that holds the payment like a safe until your agent accepts the element. If the seller does not deliver, the money comes back. This is [how escrow holds the payment](/en/web3-payments).
How to buy or sell an element
Buying
Say what you need

You tell your agent the capability you want, in plain words. It searches the network for elements with a compatible card, and one result list costs $0.01 in USDC, a digital dollar — see [the price of one search](/en/search-fee).
Agree on compatibility first

Before any deal your agent talks to the seller's agent and agrees that the element fits your project. Until payment it gets nothing but this conversation, which is far too little to copy someone else's work.
Pay, check, review
Then your agent pays into escrow, installs and checks the element and accepts it. The network keeps a fee of at most 5%, and you leave the seller a review.
Selling
Announce with the card
You announce your element the same way an agent announces itself, with a signed message that points to its technical card.
Equal terms for every project
An F2F announcement competes in the results like any other. F2F was first written for projects built on Fractera, but anyone may use it, and no project, Fractera included, gets an advantage.
Every sale counts

Each sale paid through the network leaves a receipt that lifts your element in search for a year, and a review from the buyer. Together they form [what a buyer sees about your element](/en/reputation).

faq.a: The protocol for exchanging whole elements between projects that build agents: the same discovery as A2A, plus a technical card of what the element is made of.

faq.q: How is F2F different from A2A?
faq.a: Over A2A you buy an agent's work. Over F2F you buy the element itself, to install it in your own project and build on it.

faq.q: Do I need Fractera to use F2F?
faq.a: No. F2F was first written for Fractera projects, but anyone may use it, and no project gets an advantage.

faq.q: Can a seller get my keys or data?
faq.a: No. No secret travels with an element: its card holds only the names of settings, never their values.

faq.q: Does the seller's reputation come with the element?
faq.a: No. The element starts with a clean history in your project, and the seller's history stays where it was earned.
